strengths: First study of watermarking for diffusion language models (DLMs), addressing a timely and practically important gap as DLMs (LLaDA, Dream, Mercury) become competitive with autoregressive LLMs; existing hash-based ARLM watermarks are indeed inapplicable when context is not yet generated.

Principled formulation: the paper casts DLM watermarking as a constrained optimization problem, derives an implicit optimal solution (Theorem 3.1) via KKT conditions with a proof, and shows the formulation reduces exactly to Red-Green ARLM watermarks in the autoregressive case—this provides both theoretical grounding and a natural bridge to prior work.

Efficient practical instantiations: analytic derivations of hash distributions (SumHash via FFT convolution, MinHash via cumulative products) avoid the naive O(Σ^L) computation, and the interpretive decomposition into 'expectation boost' and 'predictive bias' terms is insightful and well-supported (App. I.2).

Extensive and well-designed evaluation: two main DLMs plus an infilling model, multiple remasking strategies, ablations over hash functions, context sets, iterations, ε/δ-parameterization, temperature, γ, top-k, diffusion steps; comparisons not only to a naive KGW baseline but also to order-agnostic watermarks (Unigram, PatternMark) and adapted AAR/KTH baselines; robustness testing with a standard attack toolkit; runtime analysis showing low overhead.

Useful practical findings, e.g., that ε-parameterization underperforms δ-parameterization (with a clear explanation of the KL-constraint limitation), that a single fixed-point iteration suffices, and that i.i.d. Bernoulli green lists make the binomial test rigorous (with hypergeometric analysis in App. F).
Good reproducibility: code release, detailed experimental setup including prompts, rejection sampling, judge system prompt, and hardware details.
weaknesses: The fixed-point iteration lacks convergence guarantees; the paper acknowledges this empirically (single iteration works best in practice), but the gap between the theoretically optimal solution (Eq. 4) and what is actually deployed (one-step, δ-parameterized approximation) weakens the significance of the optimization framework itself—the practical method deviates from the theory it is derived from.

Evaluation is largely centered on the Red-Green family; while reasonable, extension of other watermark paradigms (e.g., distortion-free or semantic watermarks) to DLMs is not explored, and the 'first watermark for DLMs' claim rests on a single watermark family.

Security analysis is qualitative rather than experimental: the paper argues robustness to scrubbing/spoofing for larger |C| by citing prior work, but no watermark-stealing or spoofing attacks are actually run against the proposed scheme.

Quality assessment relies mainly on perplexity and GPT-4O-as-judge; no human evaluation, and perplexity of watermarked DLM text is measured with an external model (Qwen2.5-32B), which may imperfectly reflect DLM output quality.

Robustness to strong adversaries (paraphrasing, back-translation) remains limited, similar to ARLM watermarks; detection requires long sequences for such attacks, so the practical advantage over ARLM watermarks in adversarial settings is incremental.

Some setup details raise questions: the use of semi-autoregressive block generation for LLaDA-8B makes the main setting closer to autoregressive than purely parallel diffusion (though remasking ablations partially address this), and repetition/rejection filtering is applied, which could interact with watermark statistics.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: watermarking diffusion language models (DLMs) is unaddressed, and the paper is plausibly the first to propose a generation-time watermark tailored to this setting, with clear motivation for why autoregressive hashing fails in the diffusion setting.

Principled formulation: casting watermarking as a constrained optimization over factorized distributions with a KL quality constraint is clean, and Theorem 3.1 (with proof in App. I) provides an implicit optimal solution with a simple exponential-tilt form; the paper also shows the ARLM case recovers the Red-Green watermark exactly (App. E), which is a satisfying consistency check.

Practical and efficient instantiation: the derivations of hash distributions for SumHash (via FFT convolution) and MinHash (via CDF differences) avoid naive O(Σ^L) computation, and the top-k approximation plus single fixed-point iteration keep the generation overhead small (App. H.1, Fig. 17).

Thorough evaluation: detection/quality trade-offs on two DLMs (LLaDA-8B, DREAM-7B) plus an infilling model (DreaMon), comparisons against multiple sensible baselines (naive KGW adaptation, AAR, KTH, Unigram, PatternMark), extensive ablations (hash scheme, components, iterations, δ/ε-parameterization, remasking strategy, temperature, diffusion steps, top-k, γ, green-list distribution), robustness to edits/paraphrasing/back-translation, runtime analysis, and full ROC curves.

Good interpretability: the decomposition into 'expectation boost' and 'predictive bias' (Sec. 3.3, App. I.2) gives an intuitive account of why the method works, and the ablation confirming both terms matter supports the optimization framing.
Code availability, detailed experimental setup, and reproducibility statements improve trust in the results.
weaknesses: No formal false-positive-rate guarantee in practice: the detector relies on i.i.d. Bernoulli green lists and binomial tests, with validity only argued under simplifying assumptions (App. F, e.g., deduplication and hash-repetition arguments); empirical FPR calibration over many independent prompts/keys is not systematically reported.

Quality impact is not negligible for all settings: for DREAM-7B the watermarked text has noticeably higher perplexity than the unwatermarked model (e.g., log PPL 2.32 vs. 1.94), and the watermarked samples in App. J.2 contain factual errors (e.g., the 'Smooth'/Rob Thomas example); the paper does not analyze whether the watermark amplifies DLM hallucination tendencies, which matters for the claimed 'minimal quality impact'.

Evaluation restricted to two ~7-8B open DLMs at a fixed temperature (0.5) with mostly random remasking; results at very low temperature or with other sampling configurations (where watermarking is hardest) are only partially covered, and there is no human evaluation of watermarked text quality.

The fixed-point procedure lacks convergence guarantees for the functional equation, and the gap between the single-iteration heuristic and the optimal solution of Theorem 3.1 is only quantified empirically; also the ε-parameterization (the theoretically motivated version) underperforms, which somewhat undercuts the KL-constrained optimization story the paper leads with.

Security analysis is limited: while the paper argues higher context sizes resist scrubbing/spoofing, no direct adversarial evaluation (watermark stealing, spoofing, or DLM-specific attacks) is performed; robustness to strong adversaries (paraphrasing/back-translation) degrades substantially at short lengths.

Some positioning claims could be tempered: 'first watermark for DLMs' rests on a narrow window of concurrent work, and comparisons to order-agnostic baselines are on their DLM adaptations rather than any published DLM-specific competitor, making it hard to gauge absolute competitiveness.

strengths: First study of watermarking for diffusion language models (DLMs) — a timely and important problem given the rapid rise of DLMs (LLaDA, Dream, Mercury), and the paper correctly identifies why autoregressive hashing-based watermarks fail in the diffusion setting (context tokens not yet determined).

Principled formulation: watermarking is cast as a constrained optimization over the factorized output distribution with a KL budget, and Theorem 3.1 gives an implicit optimal solution (exponential tilting with per-position strength), connecting the DLM watermark back to Red-Green ARLM watermarks as a special case — this gives the method a clean theoretical footing rather than ad-hoc heuristics.

The interpretation in Sec. 3.3 (expectation boost + predictive bias) is insightful, and the decomposition in App. I.2 is well worked out; it also explains the observed robustness to context-aware substitution.

Comprehensive evaluation: two main DLMs (LLaDA-8B, DREAM-7B) plus an infilling model, multiple context sets, hashing schemes, remasking strategies, temperatures, diffusion-step counts, and sequence lengths; comparisons against both naive adaptations (KGW, AAR, KTH) and genuinely order-agnostic baselines (Unigram, PatternMark), with quality measured via perplexity and GPT-4o-as-judge.

Extensive ablations (top-k, gamma, green-list distribution, epsilon vs delta parameterization, fixed-point iterations) including a rigorous justification (App. F) for using an i.i.d. Bernoulli green list with an exact binomial test, which is a nice side contribution.

Strong empirical results: >99% TPR@1% FPR with minimal quality degradation across settings, minimal generation overhead, robustness to deletion/substitution/paraphrasing/back-translation, and code availability supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Restricted to the Red-Green watermark family: the framework is derived for green-list watermarks with known detectors; extension to distortion-free or Gumbel-style watermarks (e.g., a diffusion analog of AAR beyond the naive adaptation) is not developed, so the 'first watermark for DLMs' claim is limited to one family.

Security concerns acknowledged but not attacked: with the recommended C={-1}, low-context watermarks are known to be vulnerable to spoofing/scrubbing (Jovanovic et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), and the paper relies on prior work rather than empirically evaluating these attacks against the proposed scheme; no adaptive adversaries are considered beyond paraphrasing.

Convergence of the fixed-point iteration to the solution of the functional equation (Eq. 4) is not theoretically guaranteed — the authors note this and show one iteration works in practice, but the gap between the theoretical optimum and the practical algorithm is not closed.

Theorem 3.1 establishes existence of an optimal tilt form and uniqueness of delta, but the proof assumes KKT conditions apply at a maximum and does not address non-uniqueness/multiplicity of q* or the well-posedness of the joint (q*, delta) system; also the claimed uniqueness of delta_t relies on monotonicity that is asserted rather than shown in detail.

Quality evaluation relies mainly on log perplexity (measured by a third-party LLM) and GPT-4o judge scores; no human evaluation or downstream task metrics, and the KL-constraint formulation is shown to be a poor proxy for quality (Fig. 4), which somewhat undermines the epsilon-parameterized theoretical framework the paper builds up.

Experiments are limited to two open ~7-8B DLMs at moderate temperature (T=0.5, with infilling at T=0.8); the watermark weakens at low temperature and cannot be applied at T=0, and larger/frontier DLMs are not tested, leaving practical applicability at scale open.

Some results are somewhat expected or marginal: performance with autoregressive remasking is close to standard KGW, hashing choice has no significant impact, and additional fixed-point iterations help only marginally — the ablations are thorough but several components add complexity without much benefit.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: identifies a genuine limitation of autoregressive red-green watermarks in the diffusion setting (hashing requires previously generated context) and provides the first watermarking scheme tailored to diffusion language models.

Principled formulation: casting DLM watermarking as a constrained optimization problem with an implicit solution (Theorem 3.1) is elegant, and the decomposition into 'expectation boost' and 'predictive bias' terms gives useful intuition; the framework provably recovers KGW-style ARLM watermarks as a special case, which strengthens the theoretical grounding.

Comprehensive evaluation: detection-quality trade-offs across two DLMs (LLaDA-8B, DREAM-7B) plus an infilling model, multiple baselines (naive KGW adaptation, AAR, KTH, GaussMark, Unigram, PatternMark), extensive ablations (hashing scheme, components, iterations, parameterization, temperature, remasking strategy, diffusion steps, green-list distribution), robustness to local edits, paraphrasing, and back-translation.

Careful statistical treatment: i.i.d. Bernoulli green lists enabling exact binomial tests, analysis of Type-1 error control vs. Unigram, and a security discussion of spoofing/scrubbing relative to order-agnostic watermarks.

Practical considerations addressed: runtime analysis, an optimized implementation, F1 control at ~99% TPR@1 with limited perplexity and benchmark degradation, and code release supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The practical algorithm relies on a single step of a fixed-point iteration with no convergence guarantees for Eq. (4); while ablations show diminishing returns, the gap between the practical scheme and the theoretically optimal solution is not formally characterized.

The main theorem is a fairly direct Lagrangian/KKT argument; the theoretical depth is moderate, and the framework is specifically instantiated for red-green style watermarks rather than a general watermark family.

Quality impact on downstream benchmarks is inconsistent: for LLaDA-8B, the baseline preserves accuracy better than the proposed method at some settings (Table 3), and the accuracy drop at low temperature is acknowledged but not fully resolved; perplexity (measured by an external model) and GPT-4o-as-judge may not capture all quality dimensions.

Evaluation is limited to a handful of relatively small DLMs (7-8B) and English instruction/infilling tasks; scaling behavior, other languages, and stronger adaptive adversaries beyond paraphrasing/back-translation are not explored.

The recommendation of delta-parameterization over the KL-constrained formulation somewhat undermines the original constrained-optimization framing, since the epsilon-formulation is shown to be suboptimal in practice.
Security analysis is largely qualitative (reliance on prior work's attacks); no empirical spoofing/scrubbing experiments are run against the proposed watermark itself.

strengths: Identifies and formally frames a genuinely new problem: watermarking diffusion language models, where autoregressive hashing-based watermarks fail because context tokens may be unmasked after the target token. The paper is convincingly the first to address this setting.

The constrained-optimization formulation (maximize expected green ratio subject to a per-position KL budget) is clean and yields a closed-form solution (Theorem 3.1) analogous to the exponential-tilting of Red-Green watermarks, providing conceptual unification: the Red-Green ARLM watermark is recovered as a special case (App. E).

The decomposition of the resulting distortion into an 'expectation boost' and a 'predictive bias' term (Sec. 3.3) gives a valuable intuitive interpretation of why optimizing over the distribution of context hashes helps, and explains robustness to context-aware edits.

Extensive and well-organized evaluation: multiple DLMs (LLaDA-8B, DREAM-7B, DreamOn-7B for infilling), multiple remasking strategies, temperature and diffusion-step ablations, comparison against adapted baselines (KGW, Unigram, PatternMark, AAR, KTH, GaussMark), robustness tests including paraphrasing/back-translation, benchmark-accuracy and GPT-4o-as-judge quality measurements, and runtime analysis.

Notable statistical care: switching from correlated to i.i.d. Bernoulli green lists to make the binomial test exactly valid, analysis of the variance correction for the z-score detector, and an empirical Type-I error study showing Unigram's unreliable FPR versus the proposed scheme's well-controlled FPR.

Practical considerations are addressed, including an optimized implementation with negligible generation overhead, top-k approximation ablations, and concrete hyperparameter recommendations for practitioners.
weaknesses: No convergence guarantee for the fixed-point iteration used to solve the functional equation (Eq. 4). The paper relies on a single iteration in practice and only shows empirically that more iterations 'slightly' help; a theoretical justification or at least a characterization of when one iteration suffices is missing.

The ε-parameterization is theoretically principled, but the paper itself concludes that δ-parameterization is better in practice because the KL budget is a poor proxy for quality. This leaves a gap between the optimization theory (a central claimed contribution) and what is actually deployed, and the mechanism behind the KL-vs-quality mismatch is discussed only informally.

There are no theoretical guarantees on watermark strength or detectability under the DLM setting. Unlike distortion-free ARLM watermarks (e.g., Kuditipudi et al.), the paper offers no bound relating the KL budget ε to expected green-ratio gain, so the 99% TPR claims rest entirely on empirical evaluation on two main models.

Security is claimed (Sec. 4.4, App. B) by analogy to the KGW detector and to results for larger context sizes, but no spoofing or scrubbing attacks are actually run against the proposed watermark; the security comparison with order-agnostic watermarks is thus argued rather than demonstrated.

Benchmark accuracy results are somewhat noisy and mixed (e.g., the proposed watermark drops LLaDA-8B MMLU/MMBPB more than the baseline in Table 3, and a ~9-13 point drop on some benchmarks under entropy remasking in Table 4), which weakens the 'minimal quality impact' narrative; per-benchmark variance/confidence intervals are not provided.

Evaluation is limited to ~8B-parameter open DLMs and 600 prompts per setting; all baselines are adaptations by the authors rather than native methods, so fair hyperparameter tuning of competitors (e.g., KTH, GaussMark) is difficult to verify, and results on larger or proprietary DLMs remain unknown.

The no self-hashing assumption is central to making h_t computable, yet only a single simple self-hashing scheme (App. H) is evaluated; the practical impact of this restriction on broader context designs is not explored.

strengths: Addresses a timely and clearly significant problem: as diffusion LLMs (LLaDA, Dream, etc.) gain traction, existing autoregressive hashing-based watermarks become inapplicable; this appears to be the first practical watermark tailored to DLMs, which will likely be a foundational reference for this sub-area.

The paper is technically substantive rather than heuristic: watermarking is formulated as a constrained optimization problem (Eq. 1-3), Theorem 3.1 gives an implicit solution via logits shifts, and the practical scheme is rigorously connected back to Red-Green ARLM watermarks (App. E), including recovering the classic KGW scheme in the autoregressive limit. The decomposition into 'expectation boost' and 'predictive bias' terms (Sec. 3.3) provides genuine insight into why the method works.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: detection/quality trade-offs (TPR@1, PPL, GPT-4 judge, benchmark accuracy) across two DLMs plus an infilling model, robustness to local edits, paraphrasing, and back-translation, component ablations (hashing scheme, both bias terms, iterations, epsilon vs delta parameterization), comparisons to a broad set of baselines (naive ARLM adaptation, Unigram, PatternMark, AAR, KTH, GaussMark), and runtime analysis with an optimized implementation.

The statistical analysis is careful: switching to i.i.d. Bernoulli green lists to make the binomial test exact, empirical FPR calibration experiments (Fig. 7, Table 2), and a thoughtful demonstration of why order-agnostic baselines lack Type-I error control and are vulnerable to spoofing/scrubbing.

The paper is honest about trade-offs, e.g., acknowledging accuracy drops on some benchmarks for DREAM-7B, the KL vs delta parameterization discussion, and the temperature-dependence findings in the appendix. Code availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely an adaptation of the Red-Green watermarking paradigm rather than a fundamentally new watermarking principle; the main insight (optimizing over expected context hashes instead of realized hashes) is elegant but the detector and overall design remain close to KGW.

Evaluation is limited to two main open-weight DLMs of moderate scale (8B/7B) plus one infilling variant; results on a wider, larger, or commercial DLM ecosystem would strengthen the generality claims.

Some theoretical guarantees are weaker than they appear: Theorem 3.1 is an implicit characterization (existence/uniqueness), the practical algorithm uses a single fixed-point iteration without convergence guarantees, and the no-self-hashing assumption is an approximation (though empirically examined in App. H).

There are practical quality costs that are acknowledged but not fully resolved: non-negligible accuracy drops on some benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K with DREAM-7B under strong watermarking), and the method depends on sampling temperature (weak at low T, watermark inapplicable at T=0), which limits applicability to low-temperature DLM deployments.

The robustness evaluation mostly reuses standard perturbation tools from prior work; stronger adaptive attacks specifically exploiting the DLM setting or the expectation-over-hashes design are not explored.
